topic: Power Amplifiers: Class A, B and C
title: Why Amplifiers Get Hot Explained Simply | PUC Electronics Class 12
description:
At the college fest Aarav touches the big stage amplifier: it is hot and covered in metal fins, while his phone stays cool. Where does the heat come from? We compare voltage amplifiers with power amplifiers, then use a swing: one helper pushing all the time, two helpers sharing, or one short kick at the top.

On a live breadboard we turn a bias knob on a one-transistor power stage while the oscilloscope shows the collector current: class A conducts for the full 360 degrees, class B for 180 degrees, and class C in short pulses that a tuned circuit turns back into a smooth wave. The load line shows where each Q point sits, and a table compares conduction angle, maximum efficiency and distortion (with class AB in between). We derive the 25 percent maximum efficiency of a class A amplifier step by step and compare it with 50 percent (transformer coupled) and 78.5 percent (class B). A worked example shows where the heat comes from, followed by the exam trap (class C is not for music), where it is asked, an original practice question with a full solution, and a formula card to screenshot.

This is Episode 69 of PUC Electronics, Class 12, Chapter 3: Transistor Amplifiers (Karnataka II PUC Electronics). Power amplifiers are not in the rationalised NCERT/CBSE Class 12 Physics book or the current ISC Physics syllabus, so this lesson follows the Karnataka PUC Electronics syllabus.
